title: Do you believe in ghosts? Deadwood History invites public to paranormal investigation of Adams House
content:
DEADWOOD, S.D. — Rumors of the historic Adams House being haunted have existed for decades, and this weekend, the public has an opportunity to investigate.

To celebrate the spooky season of October, Deadwood History Inc. has partnered with Rapid City’s Black Hills Paranormal Investigations (BHPI) to give attendees exclusive access to “one of Deadwood’s most haunted sites.”

Investigations have taken place the previous two weekends, with the final set for Oct. 23-24. The investigations last for 90 minutes and are offered at 6 p.m., 7:30 p.m., 9 p.m. and 10:30 p.m.

Tickets are $35, and tours are limited to 24 people per investigation. Attendees must be at least 12 to participate, with ages 12 to 16 being required to be accompanied by an adult. Reservations are required.

During the event, attendees will follow along with BHPI members as they utilize digital audio recorders, laser grids, divining rods, electromagnetic fields (EMF) meters and more as they search for evidence of the paranormal.

Built in 1892, the Adams House is named after W.E. Adams, who purchased the home in 1920 and went on to become one of Deadwood’s richest and most well-known residents. Adams provided the funding for what would become the famous Adams Museum, which was completed in 1930.

In 1934, Adams suffered a stroke and died shortly after inside the home. Per the BHPI website, the first mention of its potentially haunted status comes from Adam’s second wife, Mary, as while the house was left to her, she found herself unable to live alone inside it.

After Adams’ death, Mary closed up the home and moved to California, though she continued to make annual visits to Deadwood. However, her returns saw her staying in the Franklin Hotel rather than what was once her home. When asked why she never stayed there, she claimed it was haunted.

Mary eventually sold it in 1987, with the home spending several years as a bed and breakfast. It was purchased by the city of Deadwood in 1992, which operated the bed and breakfast for a few more years before it was elected for restoration. It officially opened as a museum in 2000.

With other claims of paranormal activity emerging in the years since, the BHPI conducted multiple investigations into the home. During these investigations, BHPI staff claim to have experienced a number of strange phenomena, including what sounded like talking coming from empty rooms, footsteps coming up the stairs and whistling from other parts of the house.

BHPI was first contacted by former Deadwood History Executive Director Mary Kopco, who claimed to have witnessed paranormal activity firsthand, going as far as to say she’d even seen the ghostly apparition of Adams himself.

Those curious to browse BHPI’s collection of electronic voice phenomena recordings can do so on their website.
